newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's open-wallet sports policy hits taxpayers.
newsitem.headline: Canada's open-wallet sports policy hits taxpayers.

text.p: Canadians' love affair with professional sports is costing them much more than the price of a couple of box seats, refreshments and souvenirs.
More than C$2 billion ($1.44 billion) in taxpayers' money has been tapped since 1976 to build stadiums, prop up sports teams and enrich an exclusive club of Canadian millionaires -- sports owners.
A multitude of hockey arenas, baseball parks and even tennis courts dot the Canadian landscape, but little exists in the way of sustainable economic development.
Montreal's Olympic Stadium and Toronto's SkyDome stand as the most garish testaments to Canada's sports profligacy.
The two complexes were built in the 1970s and 1980s -- at the height of interventionist government -- and ended up costing taxpayers an eye-popping C$1.6 billion ($1.15 billion).

"The cost overruns and subsidies in Canada have become absolutely legendary," Mark Rosentraub, a public policy professor at Indiana University and author of the book on the cost of sports, "Major League Losers," said in an interview.
"Canadians have been duped into getting into the welfare business by promises that sports teams will lead to economic booms," Rosentraub said.
The so-called dupes apparently remain in abundant supply.

Officials in Hamilton, Ontario, a steel-making city hard hit by the 1990-91 recession, still pine for a National Hockey League franchise -- an enterprise that would be subsidized heavily by local taxpayers.

Montrealers, having forgotten the costly 1976 Olympic folly, are contemplating a publicly funded baseball stadium at a time when the future of major league baseball in the French-speaking city is questionable.
Not to be outdone, former Toronto Mayor David Crombie is spearheading a move to bring the 2008 Olympic games to Canada's most populous city.
"We will be 150 percent behind the bid," Jim Brown, an Ontario provincial legislator, said last summer. "The premier (Mike Harris) wants it."
Millions of Canadians believe that sports teams grease the wheels of economic growth, producing a continual spinoff of jobs and revenue.
U.S. Department of Commerce statistics, however, show that sports teams and athletic events never account for more than 0.5 percent of private sector jobs or salaries in a region.
Similar statistics for Canada do not exist, but experts flatly reject the notion that sports teams provide an additional prosperity to Canada's job-hungry cities.

Most team expenditures are on player salaries and travel, which have a negligible impact on a city's economic development, said David Whitson, a professor of sports science at the University of Alberta.
"When you give somebody from Finland C$800,000 ($572,000) to play hockey, that money will probably not stay in the local community," Whitson said.
Despite mounting skepticism, few cities are willing to buck the demands of increasingly strident sports owners.
Peter Pocklington, an Alberta sports mogul with an uncanny ability to tap the public purse, has threatened repeatedly to move the Edmonton Oilers National Hockey League team to the United States.

His demands, like those of the late Jack Kent Cooke in the United States, are heavy on daring and panache, light on economic facts. But Edmontonians more than once have dutifully passed the collection plate for the man known as Peter Puck.
In 1994 Edmonton's municipal government, along with two other governments, coughed up C$15 million ($10.8 million) to keep the Oilers in the hard-pressed city.
City officials still defend the deal.

"It's a tremendous economic benefit to be able to say you have a National Hockey League team in your city because it entices business and draws in tourists," said Terry Cavanagh, a city councilor and former mayor of Edmonton.
Cavanagh estimated the Oilers were worth about C$25 million ($17.9 million) each year in additional revenue to Edmonton businesses.
"I don't think there is any question that sports is a drawing card for this city," Cavanagh said.
